h1: Designing tap handles and tap badges that stand out on a busy bar
title: Designing Tap Handles and Tap Badges | Craft Beer School
desc: How to design tap handles and tap badges that drinkers can read on a busy bar: size, colour, information, materials and practical fit.
teaser: Your tap handle is a billboard about 60 cm from the drinker's face. Most breweries waste it.
standfirst: On a crowded bar, a tap handle or badge is often the only branding a drinker sees before ordering. We look at how to design them to be read from a distance, survive daily use and actually help sell the beer.
sections:
In a busy bar with ten or twenty taps, drinkers often choose by looking at the row of handles. A clear, distinctive handle gets noticed. A generic black handle with a small sticker gets ignored. In a guest tap setting, where your beer sits next to rivals, the handle is a big part of how you compete.

In your own taproom, handles and badges also help staff pour the right beer quickly and help regulars spot what is new.

Tap handles are the levers drinkers see. Shaped or tall handles stand out but cost more and can be heavy. Standard handles screw onto the faucet lever, typically with a 3/8 inch 16 thread on common faucets, so check your faucets before ordering.

Tap badges or lenses are smaller discs or plates on the font or the handle itself, often swappable. Many Indian taprooms use a fixed tower with badges because they are cheaper and quicker to change when the tap list rotates.

A heavy custom handle can stress the faucet lever over time and make it harder to pour gently. Keep handles reasonably light and balanced.
Design for reading at a distance

The drinker is usually standing a metre or two away, in dim light, often in a crowd. Design for that, not for a screen at arm's length.

  • One clear name. The beer name in large, simple type. Script fonts and thin lines vanish at distance.
  • Style and ABV. Below the name in smaller but still readable type. These are the two things most drinkers want next.
  • Strong contrast. Light text on dark or dark on light. Avoid mid-tones on mid-tones.
  • Distinct colours by beer or style. A consistent colour system helps people find their favourite quickly.
  • Your brewery mark in a fixed position, so your range reads as a family.

Check the design under bar lighting. Gloss finishes can glare under spotlights and make text unreadable from some angles.

If your range rotates, design a template: same shape, same layout, with a changeable colour and name panel. This keeps the bar looking organised and makes new badges cheap and quick to produce. A modular identity system makes this easy, because the rules for colour, type and logo placement already exist.

For core beers, a distinctive permanent handle can be worth the cost. For seasonals and specials, a swappable badge or insert keeps costs down.

Bar environments are hard on materials. Handles get grabbed with wet hands, wiped with cleaning chemicals and knocked during busy service. In humid Indian bars, cheap prints peel and paper inserts curl.

  • Choose wipe-clean surfaces and inks that resist cleaning sprays.
  • Avoid sharp edges that catch hands.
  • For printed badges, a protective clear layer helps them last.
  • Keep a few spares of core beer badges, because they break or go missing.

Handles can also double as merchandise. Some drinkers like to collect them. A few spare handles sold at the taproom can cover part of the cost.

When your beer goes to other bars, send handles or badges with the first keg and show staff how to fit them. Many guest bars will not have space for a large custom handle, so provide a smaller badge as well. Agree that your handle comes off when your beer runs out, so drinkers are not disappointed.

Check that your handle and badge fit the venue's overall look. A bar with a clear design style may limit what goes on its taps. See our guide to taproom design that sells for how the whole bar works together.

Make a cheap prototype first, by printing the design and taping it to an existing handle. Stand where a customer would stand, in the bar's real light. See whether you can read the name, style and ABV. Ask a few people who do not know the beers to pick one by looking. If they squint or ask staff, simplify.

Getting tap design right is part of packaging and branding work as a whole: the same thinking that makes a can readable on a shelf makes a handle readable on a bar.
faqs: What size thread do tap handles use?
Many common faucets use a 3/8 inch 16 thread for handles, but check your own faucets before ordering custom handles.
Should a tap badge show ABV?
Yes. The beer name, style and ABV are what most drinkers want to see at a glance.
Are custom tap handles worth the cost?
For core beers in busy guest bars, often yes. For rotating seasonals, a swappable badge or insert is usually more practical.
